title: Engineering documentation
headline: Ship the code. Share the context.
description: Keep architecture decisions, runbooks and setup guides beside your code. Publish them where the rest of the company can read them.
example:
# Why we chose a queue

## Decision
Process jobs asynchronously.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  API --> Queue --> Worker
```

## Trade-off
Retries must be idempotent.
pain: The implementation changes in a pull request. The explanation is still in a wiki someone has to update by hand. Soon, the two tell different stories.
payoff: Review documentation alongside code, then publish the approved Markdown to Confluence. Engineers keep their repository workflow; teammates get a page they can find and discuss.
steps: Write beside the code
Keep runbooks and decisions in a docs folder. Use Markdown links, diagrams and code examples.
Review the change
Review source in a pull request. Configure your GitHub workflow to publish after the branch or approval conditions you choose.
Publish the page tree
The publisher maps selected folders to Confluence pages and records page IDs for future updates.
benefits: Context travels with the change
The documentation source lives in the same review workflow as the implementation.
Diagrams stay editable
Mermaid source stays in Git while readers see rendered diagrams in Confluence.
Check before publishing
Validate offline, inspect a read-only plan, and keep JSON reports with your CI run.
limit: Your workflow decides when publishing runs. Commit the generated page IDs or otherwise retain the updated source between runs. Confluence edits are not automatically merged back into Git.

title: Obsidian knowledge sharing
audience: For people who think in notes
headline: Your vault is personal. Your insights don’t have to be.
description: Turn selected Obsidian notes into useful team knowledge without asking everyone to adopt your writing tools.
example:
---
connie-publish: true
tags: [team-knowledge]
---
# Project context

[[Architecture decision]]

![[Research#Key findings]]

> [!tip] Start here
> Read the decision before the details.
pain: Your best thinking is connected across notes, links and snippets. Sharing it means pasting fragments into a different editor and rebuilding the context.
payoff: Choose the notes your team needs, publish them to Confluence, and keep writing in Obsidian. Linked pages, selected embeds and attachments make the journey with them.
steps: Choose what leaves your vault
Use a publishing folder, matching tags or explicit frontmatter. Set connie-publish: false on scanned notes you want to exclude.
Keep the useful connections
Publish linked targets together and reuse whole notes or selected headings and blocks.
Share and update
Publish from the desktop plugin. Make your next edit in Markdown and publish again when it is ready.
benefits: Share a selection
You decide the publishing set rather than moving your whole vault.
Bring the context
Supported wikilinks and embeds connect the pages readers need.
Control the publish
Exclude folders or cancel after the active request; completed writes remain.
limit: The plugin runs in desktop Obsidian and is installed from release assets. Selected embeds include their content in the published note; review included sections as well as the publishing selection.

title: Research & mathematics
headline: Share the reasoning. Keep the equations.
description: Publish mathematical notes, technical diagrams and evaluated research tables as readable Confluence pages.
example:
# Model notes

Energy is $E=mc^2$.

$$
\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2}
$$

## References
[[Papers/Measurement study]]
pain: A technical explanation needs more than paragraphs. Equations, diagrams and research tables lose their meaning when you have to flatten or rebuild them in another editor.
payoff: Keep LaTeX and diagrams in source. Version 7 renders equations locally and publishes the results as attachments. In Obsidian, supported Dataview queries can publish as native tables, lists and tasks.
steps: Write the technical source
Use dollar-delimited inline or display mathematics, Mermaid, and links to your supporting notes.
Enable research tables if needed
In Obsidian, enable Dataview and Publish Dataview results for supported TABLE, LIST or TASK queries.
Publish a readable explanation
Equations and diagrams become images; evaluated tables become Confluence content alongside your writing.
benefits: No separate equation service
Bundled MathJax renders locally without a Marketplace app or TeX installation.
Query source stays editable
Dataview evaluates again on publication, including when its Markdown dependencies change.
References stay connected
Footnotes publish with return links; structured YAML tables support explicit spans.
limit: Published equations are images, and page export cannot restore their editable TeX. Dataview results are snapshots, evaluated in Obsidian; DataviewJS, inline expressions and live interactive views are not supported.

title: Team handbooks & runbooks
audience: For teams that repeat good practice
headline: Write the useful bit once. Put it where it’s needed.
description: Build onboarding guides and runbooks from reusable Markdown sections, with a page hierarchy your team can navigate.
example:
# Welcome to the team

![[Shared setup#Access checklist]]

> [!note] Need a hand?
> Ask the platform team.

```toc
```

## First week
- [ ] Read the service runbook
pain: The same access checklist appears in five guides. An update means hunting down copies, and readers are never sure which version is current.
payoff: Reuse a whole note, heading or block in multiple source pages. Publish the affected pages to bring the shared content into each destination, with folder notes and a table of contents to help readers find their way.
steps: Create shared sections
Store repeated instructions in a source note and embed only the heading or block each guide needs.
Give the handbook a structure
Use folders and folder notes for landing pages. Add a TOC, callouts and visible frontmatter properties.
Republish affected guides
Update the shared source and publish the pages that include it. Keep the Markdown files as the maintained source.
benefits: Fewer source copies to maintain
One shared section can supply multiple Markdown guides.
Consistent page context
Apply a common header or footer to source pages when the same information belongs everywhere.
Keep editing with your source
Optionally restrict editing to the publishing account while preserving viewing restrictions.
limit: Embeds are expanded during publication, not live transclusions in Confluence. Changes reach a destination when that page is published again. Markdown files and rendered content still need a clear owner.

title: Release updates & team blogs
headline: Let the work become the update.
description: Publish release notes and project updates from Markdown as Confluence blog posts, with labels and attachments.
example:
---
connie-publish: true
connie-content-type: blogpost
connie-blog-post-date: "2026-09-08"
tags: [release-notes]
---
# September update

## Shipped
- Inline and display equations
- Confluence page export
pain: Release notes are drafted near the work, then copied into a second place for the wider team. The final publishing step becomes another manual chore.
payoff: Mark a Markdown note as a blog post and publish it into a Confluence space with Blogs enabled. Keep updates, labels and attachments in the same repeatable workflow.
steps: Write the update
Draft a standalone Markdown file and add blog-post frontmatter with a quoted date.
Choose the destination
Configure an existing parent page in the target space and use an account with blog-post creation permission.
Publish and keep the ID
The source receives the content ID. Retain it to update the same post on later runs.
benefits: Use the right destination
A dated team update can be a blog post rather than another page in a handbook.
Label the update
YAML tags become Confluence labels that travel with the published content.
Bring the demo
Local MP4 embeds publish as attachment media groups alongside release notes.
limit: Blogs must be enabled in the destination space. A date sets blog-post metadata; it is not a future publishing scheduler. Changing an existing page’s type does not automatically migrate it to a blog post.

title: Confluence to local tools
headline: Bring a page back into your workflow.
description: Read a Confluence page into Markdown or ADF for local review, processing or reuse.
example:
vp dlx @markdown-confluence/cli@7.0.0 \
  to-markdown --page 123456 \
  --output confluence-page.md

# Prefer simpler Markdown?
# Add --readable
pain: Useful knowledge already lives in Confluence, but the next step needs a local file: a review, a conversion script, or another tool in your workflow.
payoff: Export a page by URL or ID using your existing credentials. Choose readable Markdown for people or preserve rich ADF content in lossless mode when structure matters.
steps: Identify the page
Supply its numeric ID or supported Confluence page URL. Read access and connection settings are required; a publishing parent is not.
Choose the output
Use to-markdown for Markdown, --readable for simpler output, or to-adf for the original ADF document.
Use the file locally
Review, transform or store the output. File-to-file and stdin/stdout conversion also work without Confluence credentials.
benefits: Read without changing the source page
Export is a separate read operation.
Choose the trade-off
Readable output simplifies rich content; default lossless mode preserves it in ADF fences.
Compose it into your tools
Use files, pipes or the Node.js library to fit the next step in your workflow.
limit: Export does not download attachments, migrate media IDs or recreate server-side macro objects and comments. It is not a whole-space migration or automatic two-way sync. Published equation images remain images.
